title: Four Major US Immigration Rule Changes in 2026 That Every Indian National Needs To Know
excerpt: From the end of open-ended student visas to a $100,000 H-1B fee, the Trump administration is overhauling legal immigration pathways that hundreds of thousands of Indians depend on.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • DHS caps F-1 and J-1 visas at four years, impacting 1.2 million students.
  • New public charge rule may deny green cards to those using public benefits.
  • Automatic extensions for Employment Authorization Documents are eliminated, requiring re-vetting.
  • $100,000 fee on H-1B visas starts September 21, significantly raising costs for employers.

The US immigration landscape is undergoing its most sweeping transformation in decades, and few communities stand to feel the impact as acutely as the Indian diaspora. In a series of regulatory actions, the Trump administration has rewritten the rules governing student visas, work authorisations, green card eligibility, and the H-1B programme — four pillars that underpin the lives of hundreds of thousands of Indian nationals in the United States.

https://x.com/PaulineHansonOz/status/2079742617735286807

End of Duration of Status: A Four-Year Cap on Student Visas

On July 16, the Department of Homeland Security published a final rule abolishing the "duration of status" (D/S) system that had governed F-1 student visas and J-1 exchange visas since 1978. Under D/S, international students could remain in the US for as long as they were enrolled in an approved programme. That flexibility is now gone.

Under the new framework, student and exchange visas are capped at four years. Students needing more time — common for doctoral candidates, who typically spend six to seven years on dissertations — must apply to USCIS for extensions, with background checks and fraud reviews. The rule also halves the post-graduation grace period from 60 to 30 days and transfers authority over academic transfers from universities to federal officials. It takes effect September 15, 2026.

> **"Indians hold over 70% of H-1B visas issued annually, making them the community most directly affected."**

"For nearly half a century, the outdated 'duration of status' system has compromised national security and created an environment ripe for immigration fraud."

— Markwayne Mullin, DHS Secretary

A Brookings Institution analysis estimates the regulation could cause annual losses of $72 to $145 billion to the US economy over a decade. A survey for the National Academies of Sciences found roughly half of current international PhD students said they would not have come to the US had D/S been eliminated before they enrolled.

Expanded Public Charge Rule

A second major shift arrived on July 17, when DHS published a final rule reviving the "public charge" framework for green card adjudications. Effective September 18, immigration officers can consider a wider array of public assistance — including food stamps, Medicaid, and housing vouchers — when deciding whether an applicant is likely to become dependent on government support. The rule rescinds a 2022 Biden-era regulation and affects approximately 588,000 annual applicants.

"We are reaffirming the requirement of self-reliance, protecting public resources, and ending policies that encouraged dependency on hard-working American taxpayers."

— Department of Homeland Security

DHS itself estimates roughly 950,000 people may disenroll from safety net programmes out of fear it will hurt their immigration cases — including benefits their US-citizen children are entitled to receive.

EAD Auto-Extensions Eliminated

USCIS has terminated the automatic 180-day extension of Employment Authorisation Documents for immigrants filing renewal applications. Previously, workers could continue employment while renewals were processed. Now each renewal requires complete re-vetting. USCIS Director Joseph Edlow called it a "commonsense measure," but processing delays that can stretch months could leave workers temporarily unemployed through no fault of their own.

The $100,000 H-1B Fee

Perhaps the most headline-grabbing change is a presidential proclamation imposing a $100,000 fee on every new H-1B visa petition filed after September 21, 2026 — replacing a fee structure that cost employers roughly $1,500. Indians hold over 70% of H-1B visas issued annually, making them the community most directly affected. Current holders are unaffected, but the cost could fundamentally alter hiring decisions for mid-sized IT firms and startups that rely on Indian talent.

India Watches Closely

Timeline of Immigration Rule Changes
July 16, 2026
DHS ends 'duration of status' for student visas.
September 15, 2026
New four-year cap on student visas takes effect.
September 18, 2026
Expanded public charge rule becomes effective.
September 21, 2026
New $100,000 H-1B fee implemented.
DHS announcements

New Delhi has said it is "actively monitoring" the situation. MEA spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal confirmed India is in contact with Washington and "will consistently advocate for genuine students and travellers facing hurdles." The Cato Institute's David Bier has questioned the legal basis for the student visa restrictions, and press freedom groups have flagged journalist visa caps as potential tools for editorial retaliation.

With three of the four rules taking effect in September 2026, the coming months represent a critical window for Indian students, H-1B professionals, and families navigating the green card process.
